groups.en: Onkelos explains the disclosure of Sedom's judgment, the paths of righteousness and justice Avraham's household must keep, and the possibility of repentance. 'I shall descend' is rendered as revelation and judgment, not bodily movement.
groups.he: האונקלוס מבאר את גילוי דין סדום, את דרכי הצדקה והמשפט שעל בית אברהם לשמור, ואת האפשרות לתשובה. ׳ארדה׳ מתורגם כגילוי ודיון, ולא כתיאור תנועה גופנית.

groups.en: Avraham is portrayed as standing in prayer. His plea distinguishes innocent from guilty and seeks forgiveness for the place on account of the righteous; Onkelos emphasizes the truth of the Creator's judgments.
groups.he: אברהם מתואר כעומד בתפילה. בקשתו מבדילה בין צדיק לרשע ומבקשת סליחה למקום בזכות הצדיקים, ואונקלוס מדגיש את אמיתת משפטי הבורא.

groups.en: The Targum calls Elisha the prophet of ה׳ and follows the promise of a son, his birth, illness, and death. The closing of the room at the end leaves the mother's further action to the next reading.
groups.he: התרגום מכנה את אלישע נביא ה׳ ומלווה את הבטחת הבן, לידתו, מחלתו ומותו. סגירת החדר בסוף הקטע משאירה את המשך פעולת האם לקריאה הבאה.

groups.en: The mother sets out to the prophet without immediately disclosing the disaster to her husband or Elisha's attendant. 'Peace' is her answer within the narrative, not the narrator's assertion that the boy is healthy.
groups.he: האם יוצאת אל הנביא ואינה מגלה מיד את האסון לבעלה או לנערו של אלישע. ׳שלום׳ הוא תשובתה בתוך הסיפור; אין להפוך אותו לקביעה של המספר שהילד בריא.

groups.en: Wisdom is portrayed as one to acquire, love, and embrace, guarding and honoring the learner. Acquisition here is not limited to money; it describes making wisdom and understanding durably one's own.
groups.he: החכמה מתוארת כדמות שיש לקנות, לאהוב ולחבק, והיא שומרת ומכבדת את הלומד. לשון הקנייה אינה מוגבלת לכסף אלא מתארת היקלטות יציבה של חכמה ובינה.

groups.en: The passage moves from listening and guidance to holding fast to discipline and avoiding the wicked's paths. The unconfined path represents conduct that does not cause stumbling, even when one moves quickly.
groups.he: הקטע מתקדם מהקשבה והדרכה אל אחיזה במוסר והתרחקות מדרכי הרשעים. הדרך הרחבה מייצגת הליכה שאינה מכשילה, גם כשהאדם ממהר.

groups.en: Metzudas Dovid explains the time of birth, the woman's fear of joy that will not endure, and the child's pain. Its reading of the appointed time concerns giving birth and the months of pregnancy; it should not be merged with Rashi's reading concerning the woman's remaining alive and well.
groups.he: מצודת דוד מבאר את מועד הלידה, את חששה של האשה משמחה שאינה מתקיימת ואת כאב הילד. פירושו לאמירת ׳כעת חיה׳ עוסק ביולדת ובחודשי ההריון, ואין למזגו עם פירוש רש״י על קיום האשה בחיים ובשלום.

groups.en: Metzudas Dovid explains the urgent journey and withholding of the disaster in the hope that the miracle will occur privately. It clarifies that the attendant should continue driving the donkey until she tells him to stop.
groups.he: מצודת דוד מסביר את היציאה הדחופה ואת אי גילוי האסון מתוך מחשבה שהנס ייעשה בצנעה. הוא מבהיר שהנער ימשיך להנהיג את האתון עד שתאמר לו לעמוד.

groups.en: The commentary connects a father's love with constructive rebuke, and regular study with acquiring wisdom and understanding. Continually handling wisdom emphasizes sustained engagement with Torah, not a single act.
groups.he: הפירוש מחבר אהבת האב לתוכחה בונה, ולימוד קבוע לקניין חכמה ובינה. ׳ממשמש בה׳ מדגיש עיסוק מתמיד בתורה, ולא פעולה חד פעמית.

groups.en: Calling the learner 'my son' expresses affection and a desire for his improvement. Years of life are explained as good and tranquil years; guidance on a straight path continues in an unrelenting grip on discipline.
groups.he: הפנייה ׳בני׳ מבטאת חיבה ורצון בתיקון הלומד. שנות החיים מתפרשות כשנים טובות ושלוות, וההדרכה בדרך ישרה נמשכת באחיזה שאינה מרפה מן המוסר.

groups.en: Mizrachi traces the scriptural grounds of Rashi's wording: accompanying the guests, the two functions of 'so that,' and the difference between sin already committed and persisting in rebellion. He also records textual differences in the Midrash about a righteous son.
groups.he: המזרחי עוקב אחר הראיות שבפסוק ללשון רש״י: ליווי האורחים, שני תפקידי ׳למען׳, וההבחנה בין חטא שכבר נעשה לבין עמידה במרד. הוא גם מציג הבדלי נוסח במדרש על בן צדיק.

groups.en: Maskil LeDavid examines charity and tithes, offers answers to the objections about looking down, and explains why Rashi places Midrash before plain meaning. He does not conceal the difficulties remaining in both interpretations of 'I shall descend.'
groups.he: משכיל לדוד בוחן את היחס בין צדקה ומעשרות, מציע תשובות לקושיות על ׳השקפה׳, ומבאר מדוע רש״י מביא מדרש לפני פשט. הוא אינו מטשטש את הקשיים שנותרים בשתי דרכי פירוש ׳ארדה׳.

groups.en: Chizkuni raises objections to the rule about looking down, explains Avraham's view of his guests as prophets, and connects disclosure of Sedom's judgment with educating his household. 'I shall know' is explained through mercy.
groups.he: חזקוני מציג קושיות על כלל ׳כל השקפה לרעה׳, מבהיר את הכרת אברהם באורחים כנביאים, וקושר את הודעת דין סדום לחינוך ביתו. ׳אדעה׳ מתבאר ברחמים.

groups.en: Rashbam distinguishes the two angels going to Sedom from the third who speaks with Avraham. In his interpretation, the use of ה׳ in these verses is connected with the angel's commission; this is not the reading shared by all commentators.
groups.he: רשב״ם מבחין בין שני המלאכים היוצאים לסדום לבין השלישי המדבר עם אברהם. לפי פירושו, כינוי ה׳ בפסוקים אלה קשור לשליחות המלאך; אין זו אותה קריאה של כל המפרשים.

groups.en: Gur Aryeh explains the force of gifts to the poor, Avraham's love for the spiritual promises, and the language of descending and seeing. He keeps the region's outcry distinct from the interpretation of the young woman's cry.
groups.he: גור אריה מבאר את כוח מתנות העניים, את אהבת אברהם להבטחות הרוחניות ואת לשון הירידה והראייה. הוא מציג בנפרד את פירוש צעקת המדינה ואת דרשת צעקת הנערה.

groups.en: Mizrachi analyzes the narrative sequence and 'scribal adjustment,' Avraham's three modes of approach, and the move from saving the place to saving the righteous. He distinguishes actual judgment from the mistaken impression people might form of it.
groups.he: המזרחי מנתח את סדר הסיפור ואת ׳תיקון סופרים׳, את שלוש דרכי פניית אברהם ואת מעברו מהצלת המקום להצלת הצדיקים. הוא מבחין בין אמת הדין לבין הרושם המוטעה שעלול להיווצר אצל הבריות.

groups.en: Levush HaOrah preserves Mizrachi's objection and disputes Gur Aryeh's answer about 'still.' In interpreting 'the world to come,' he proposes concern for desecration of the Name also in the eyes of the righteous there, not only in this world.
groups.he: לבוש האורה משמר את קושיית המזרחי וחולק על תשובת גור אריה בעניין ׳עודנו׳. בפירוש ׳לעולם הבא׳ הוא מציע חשש לחילול השם גם בעיני הצדיקים שבעולם הבא, ולא רק בעולם הזה.

groups.en: Rashbam continues his reading of standing before the angel and entreating him. He explains 'sweep away' as destruction and identifies Sedom as the center of the area's kingdoms.
groups.he: רשב״ם ממשיך את פירושו על עמידה לפני המלאך ובקשת פניו. הוא מסביר את ׳תספה׳ בלשון כילוי ואת מעמד סדום כמרכז מלכויות המקום.

groups.en: Gur Aryeh offers a particular analysis of 'still' and the Torah's respectful language, and connects Avraham's three approaches with three attributes. His discussion of desecration of the Name concerns human perception and the elevation of justice, not permission for injustice.
groups.he: גור אריה מציע ניתוח מסוים של ׳עודנו׳ ושל לשון הכבוד שבתורה, ומחבר את שלוש דרכי אברהם לשלוש מידות. דיונו בחילול השם עוסק בתפיסת הבריות ובמעלת המשפט, ולא בהיתר לעוול.

groups.en: Maskil LeDavid proposes a different version of Rashi's example of conciliation and distinguishes physical approach from the interpretation of 'he approached.' He also discusses the force of ten and the two pleas of 'far be it,' without harmonizing them with every other commentator's view.
groups.he: משכיל לדוד מציע גרסה אחרת לדוגמת הפיוס שבדברי רש״י ומבחין בין התקרבות גופנית לבין דרשת ׳ויגש׳. הוא דן גם בכוחם של עשרה ובשתי בקשות ׳חלילה׳ בלי ליישב אותן עם כל שיטות שאר המפרשים.

groups.en: Chizkuni identifies the principal city as Sedom and understands 'the world to come' here as coming generations. His brief note on 'to You' concerns language and vocalization, not a new discussion of Names or bodies.
groups.he: חזקוני מזהה את העיר המרכזית כסדום ומבאר ׳לעולם הבא׳ כדורות הבאים. הערתו הקצרה על ׳לך׳ היא הערת לשון וניקוד, ולא דיון חדש בשמות או בגופים.

groups.en: Ramban distinguishes speech addressed to the heavenly host or angels from saying that denotes inward thought. Both possibilities are retained in his commentary.
groups.he: הרמב״ן מבחין בין אמירה לצבא השמים או למלאכים לבין אמירה שהיא מחשבה פנימית. שתי האפשרויות נשמרות בפירושו.

groups.en: Ramban does not stop at a blessing occasioned by mentioning Avraham. Revealing the judgment to him prevents a false impression of the Creator's conduct or of Avraham's compassion, and makes possible a prayer grounded in righteousness and justice.
groups.he: הרמב״ן אינו מסתפק בברכה אגב הזכרת אברהם. גילוי הדין לאברהם מונע רושם מוטעה על הנהגת הבורא ועל רחמי אברהם, ומאפשר תפילה המיוסדת על צדקה ומשפט.

groups.en: Ramban presents several readings of 'I have known him' and 'so that,' and finally emphasizes continual individual providence over the pious as distinct from preservation of general classes in the lower world.
groups.he: הרמב״ן מציג כמה פירושים ל׳ידעתיו׳ ול׳למען׳, ולבסוף מדגיש השגחה פרטית מתמדת בחסידים לעומת שמירת הכללים בעולם השפל.

groups.en: Ramban offers alternative narrative sequences, identifies the outcry as that of the oppressed, and distinguishes the plain sense of coming to judge from the interpretation of a passage from mercy to judgment. Avraham's prayer belongs within that judgment, not within ignoring the innocence or guilt of those judged.
groups.he: הרמב״ן מציע סדרי סיפור חלופיים, מבאר את צעקת העשוקים, ומפריד בין פשט הירידה לשפוט לבין דרשת המעבר ממידת הרחמים למידת הדין. תפילת אברהם משתלבת בבירור הדין ולא בהעלמת צדקתם או רשעתם של הנידונים.

groups.en: Ramban distinguishes judgment from mercy, explaining the repeated 'far be it from You' and the different Names in Avraham's address and the Creator's reply.
groups.he: הרמב״ן מבחין בין מידת הדין למידת הרחמים ומבאר את כפל ׳חלילה לך׳ ואת השמות השונים שבפי אברהם ובתשובת הבורא.

groups.en: Ramban sets out Rashi's view, challenges it, and attempts to explain it, then prefers a plain reading in which Avraham seeks to save all the cities at every stage. The attempted explanation must not be portrayed as his final agreement.
groups.he: הרמב״ן מציג את שיטת רש״י במלואה, מקשה עליה ומנסה לבארה, ואחר כך מעדיף פשט שלפיו אברהם ביקש להציל את כל הערים בכל שלב. אין להציג את ניסיון הביאור כהסכמה הסופית שלו.

groups.en: Ramban cites the interpretation of public fear of God, but prefers to read 'within the city' as including strangers such as Lot whose merit might save the place.
groups.he: הרמב״ן מביא את פירוש היראה בפרהסיה, ומעדיף לפרש ש׳בתוך העיר׳ כולל גם זרים כמו לוט שזכותם עשויה להציל את המקום.

groups.en: This is a lemma only. The reading receives a translation of the words actually supplied, without inventing an exposition in Rashi's name.
groups.he: זהו דיבור מתחיל בלבד. הקריאה מקבלת תרגום של המילים שנמסרו, בלי ליצור בשמו של רש״י פירוש שאינו בשדה המקור.

groups.en: The Zohar interprets the written לא and the read לו to speak about the Shechinah accompanying Israel in distress and exile. It then connects remembrance of the covenant and the particle את with images of the Patriarchs' union and of day and night. These interpretations and directions belong to the passage's symbolic language; they are not a new Name diagram or practical meditation instruction.
groups.he: הזוהר דורש את הכתיב ׳לא׳ והקרי ׳לו׳ כדי לדבר על ליווי השכינה לישראל בצרה ובגלות. אחר כך הוא קושר את זכירת הברית ואת מילת ׳את׳ לדימויי איחוד האבות ויום ולילה. הדרשות והכיוונים הם לשון סמלית של הקטע, ולא מפת שמות או הוראת כוונה מעשית חדשה.

groups.en: The passage distinguishes the prohibition of unfair pricing from three monetary consequences: a discrepancy below one sixth, one of a sixth, and one above a sixth. In the last case the right to undo the transaction belongs to the injured party, not to the party seeking to profit from the unfair price. This is study of the abridged classical passage, not a practical ruling covering all the conditions of these laws.
groups.he: הקטע מבדיל בין איסור אונאה לבין שלוש תוצאות ממוניות: פחות משתות, שתות ויותר משתות. הזכות לחזור במקרה האחרון ניתנת למתאנה, ולא למאנה המבקש להרוויח מעוולתו. זהו לימוד הקטע הקלאסי המקוצר, ולא הכרעה מעשית בכל פרטי דיני אונאה.

groups.en: The teaching links respectful speech, patience, and restraint in anger to the images of carrying a burden and wearing a garment of light. The lost coin and broken vessel illustrate the folly of sacrificing a precious spiritual bond over a passing loss. Its severe language is historical moral exhortation, not a diagnosis of grief, depression, or a medical condition.
groups.he: המוסר קושר כבוד בדיבור, סבלנות וזהירות בכעס לדימוי של נשיאת משא ולבוש אור. משל הפרח והכלי מדגיש שאין לאבד קשר רוחני יקר בגלל הפסד חולף. לשון החומרה כאן היא דברי מוסר היסטוריים, ולא אבחון של צער, דיכאון או מצב רפואי.

groups.en: The three paragraphs prohibit even temporary or playful taking, apply the prohibition irrespective of the owner's communal identity or age, and distinguish secret theft from open robbery. The final distinction concerns legal classification; it does not permit taking property openly.
groups.he: שלושת הסעיפים אוסרים גם לקיחה זמנית או לשם משחק, משווים את איסור הגניבה לפי זהות בעל הממון וגילו, ומבחינים בין גנב בסתר לגזלן בגלוי. ההבחנה האחרונה היא בסיווג המשפטי, ואינה היתר לקחת ממון בגלוי.

groups.en: The passage addresses the sinner in severe language of rebuke and seeks to redirect fear of other people toward awe of the Creator. It does not establish that every poor or suffering person is a sinner, and it must not be turned into an instruction for a victim to remain silent, stay in danger, or forgo help and protection.
groups.he: הקטע פונה אל החוטא בלשון תוכחה חריפה ומבקש להפנות את פחד האדם מבני אדם אל יראת הבורא. אין זו קביעה שכל עני או סובל הוא חוטא, ואין להסיק ממנה הוראה לנפגע לשתוק, להישאר בסכנה או לוותר על סיוע והגנה.

rows.he: אֲרֵי גְּלִי קֳדָמַי (גי' רמב''ן יְדַעְתִּנֵּהּ) בְּדִיל דִּי יְפַקֵּד יָת בְּנוֹהִי וְיָת אֱנַשׁ בֵּיתֵהּ בַּתְרוֹהִי וְיִטְּרוּן אָרְחָן דְּתַקְּנָן קֳדָם יְיָ לְמֶעֱבַּד צְדַקְתָּא וְדִינָא בְּדִיל אַיְיתִי יְיָ עַל אַבְרָהָם יָת דְּמַלֵּל עֲלוֹהִי

rows.en: 'At this appointed time, at the time of giving birth': This means at the coming time suited for her to be a woman giving birth—that is, at the completion of nine months, which are the days of pregnancy. 'You will be embracing a son': This means you will delight in your son by embracing him. Although at first he did not speak with her face to face, after he saw her modesty in standing at the doorway, he turned to speak with her. 'No, my master': Do not speak such words. 'Do not disappoint': Do not say something that will cease to be, merely to gladden your maidservant's heart. Because he said 'embracing a son,' which indicates some enjoyment, but did not promise her that the child would endure, she therefore said: Do not gladden me with something that does not endure.
rows.he: למועד הזה כעת חיה. רצה לומר: לזמן הבא כעת הראויה להיות חיה רוצה לומר: יולדת, והיא ככלות תשעה חדשים, שהם ימי הריון: את חובקת בן. רצה לומר: תשעשע עצמך עם בנך לחבקו, ואף כי בתחלה לא דבר עמה פנים אל פנים, אבל אחר שראה צניעותה שעמדה בפתח, חזר לדבר עמה: אל אדוני. אל תדבר כדברים האלה: אל תכזב. אל תאמר דבר הנפסק, בעבור לשמח לב שפחתך, ועל כי אמר חובקת בן, המורה לשעשוע מה, ולא הבטיחה שיתקיים, לזה אמרה אל תשמחני בדבר שאינו מתקיים:

rows.en: 'Neither the new month nor Shabbos': For on the new month and on Shabbos she was accustomed to visit him. 'She said: Peace': This means there is no bad occurrence on account of which I am going to the prophet. She did not wish to reveal the matter to her husband, for she thought it better that the miracle take place in private.

rows.en: 'They looked,' and so forth; 'gifts to the poor,' and so forth: Although the verse concerns tithes, and in Chagigah, from which Rashi derived this, it likewise says, 'Great is the power of those who bring out tithes,' nevertheless, since the tithes include the poor person's tithe, Rashi understands the same to apply to all gifts to the poor. It appears that Rashi was compelled to say this because he himself perceived what Chizkuni asked against this generalization from 'Righteousness has looked down from heaven,' where it is certainly not for evil. Rashi's words answer it well: 'Righteousness has looked down from heaven' means that the commandment of charity has great power, such that from heaven He looks down to turn the attribute of anger into mercy in its merit. Chizkuni's further question from 'For He looked down from His holy height' is likewise no difficulty. There the poet prays for redemption, saying, 'Nations shall fear the name of ה׳,' and so forth; 'For He has built,' and so forth; 'He has turned toward the prayer of the destitute,' and so forth; 'For He looked down from His holy height,' and so forth; 'To hear the groaning of the prisoner,' and so forth. Indeed, it is a looking down for evil upon the enemies of our lives, to return their recompense upon their heads. Likewise, the objection from 'Who is she who looks forth like the dawn?' is no difficulty: that verse too is interpreted in Midrash Chazis concerning Israel's redemption, which resembles dawn, since at first there is darkness. It brings there the verse, 'When I sit in darkness, ה׳ is a light to me.' This fits: after being 'looked upon'—that is, amid troubles—there comes redemption, just like dawn. Furthermore, in the portion of Beshalach they interpreted this verse concerning the Babylonian exile, when, despite all Israel's troubles, they sanctified the Name of Heaven; see there. Afterward I saw that Nachalas Yaakov wrote that only the tithe is called 'gifts to the poor,' and it cannot refer to other gifts to the poor, since the Talmud explicitly says there that the merit of charity does not turn the attribute of anger into mercy; see there. With due respect, that is not so. It is true that the passage says, 'To You, ה׳, belongs righteousness,' and so forth. Rabbi Nechemyah said: Even when we give charity, we look at our deeds and are ashamed; the only time we come with a confident claim is when we bring out tithes, and so forth. From this the Rabbi inferred that Rabbi Alexandri's ensuing statement, 'Great is their power,' and so forth, applies specifically to tithes, not charity. But that does not follow from this, for afterward it says about tithes too what it said about charity, as follows: Even when we bring out our tithes, we look at our deeds, and so forth. In ordinary practice, a person gives his field to others and divides the produce equally with them, whereas the whole world belongs to the Holy One, blessed is He, and so forth, and I told you to give Me only a tithe, and so forth. Thus, 'To You, ה׳, belongs righteousness.' This is the end of the quotation. The same kind of statement that they made about charity, then, they also made about tithes.

'Every looking down is for evil,' and so forth: The reason that looking down is for evil is that it is an expression of striking. Thus a lintel is called mashkof because the door strikes against it. rows.en: 'Shall I conceal from Avraham': That I wish to overturn Sedom, while I know that his children will keep the way of ה׳ and merit that He bring upon them what He spoke to Avraham, to give them the land of Canaan? These towns are part of his children's inheritance, as it is written concerning the border of the children of Canaan in the portion of Noach: 'The border of the Canaanites was from Tzidon, as you come to Gerar, as far as Gaza; as you come toward Sedom and Amorah, Admah and Tzevoyim, as far as Lasha.' How could I destroy his land and his children's land without his knowledge?

rows.en: 'And Avraham,' and so forth; 'a Midrash of Aggadah,' and so forth; 'and its plain meaning,' and so forth: The plain meaning follows what Rashi explained in the preceding comment. But he first brings the Midrash because the plain interpretation leaves a difficulty: 'And Avraham' is superfluous. rows.en: 'It does not say upon Avraham's household, but upon Avraham,' and so forth: In Beraishis Rabbah, however, they said: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai taught that anyone who has a son who labors in Torah is as though he did not die. What is the reason? 'So that ה׳ may bring upon Avraham': It does not say 'what He spoke to him,' but 'what He spoke about him.' There are two differences here. First, there it says, 'Anyone who has a son who labors in Torah,' whereas Rashi writes, 'One who raises a righteous son.' Second, there it says, 'It does not say what He spoke to him, but what He spoke about him,' which implies that the proof sought is that it does not refer to Avraham himself. Rashi, however, writes, 'It does not say upon Avraham's household, but upon Avraham,' implying that it is already clear to him that it is not speaking of Avraham himself. I do not know whether he found this written elsewhere, or whether this was the wording in his copy of Beraishis Rabbah. However that may be, Rashi's words are the principal explanation, because 'They will keep the way of ה׳ to do righteousness and justice' concerns righteous people, not those laboring in Torah. Also, since Scripture speaks about Avraham's household, as it says, 'So that he will command his children and his household after him,' it should have written, 'So that ה׳ may bring upon Avraham's household,' instead of 'upon Avraham.' There should therefore be no uncertainty as to whether 'upon Avraham' refers to Avraham himself, requiring the inference that it does not say 'what He spoke to him,' but 'what He spoke about him.' Rather, it is certainly not speaking of Avraham himself but of his household, and Scripture calls it 'upon Avraham' as though he had not died.

'Anyone who raises a righteous son,' and so forth: The righteous are called living even in their death, and one who raises a righteous son, who is considered living even in death, is himself likewise living. rows.en: 'Another interpretation: I shall descend now to the end of their deeds': The Sages' idiom concerning profound matters is, 'I have not descended to the end of his understanding.' It appears from here that the teaching here—that judges should not decide capital cases except through seeing—and what Rashi wrote in the portion of the Dispersion—that judges should not convict the accused until they see and understand—are derived not from 'and I shall see' here or 'to see' there, but from 'descending,' like a person who descends from his seat to go see and investigate a matter. Otherwise, how could 'another interpretation: I shall descend to the end of their deeds' follow a discussion of seeing and then offer an alternative concerning descending? Moreover, Rashi should have explained 'He taught judges,' and so forth, on 'and I shall see,' not on 'I shall descend now.' Therefore the more correct explanation in my view is that the descending is interpreted according to the seeing: if the seeing is sensory, so too is the descending; if the seeing is intellectual, so too is the descending. Thus, from his interpretation of seeing as sensory we learn that the descending too is sensory; and from his interpretation of descending as intellectual we learn that the seeing too is intellectual, as in 'my heart saw.' He explained intellectual descending as descending to the end of their deeds, rather than explaining intellectual seeing as in 'my heart saw,' because intellectual seeing has many parallels in Scripture, whereas intellectual descending has no parallels anywhere in Scripture, only in the language of our Sages of blessed memory. Therefore he needed to say that descending too may be used for intellectual descent.

rows.en:
'Another interpretation,' and so forth: Here descending means reaching the end of their deeds: I shall descend to examine them closely and see into their deeds, for reaching the depth of a matter is called descending. Once the descending is intellectual, the seeing is likewise interpreted intellectually, as in 'My heart saw much wisdom.' He said, 'Another interpretation: I shall descend to the end of their deeds,' without explaining anything about the seeing, even though his first interpretation, 'He taught judges not to decide except through seeing,' concerned 'and I shall see,' not 'I shall descend.' This is because initially we were compelled to interpret the seeing as actual seeing only because of the descending written beside it. The language of descending implies actual descent. Without the language of descending, we could obviously have explained the seeing like 'My heart saw much wisdom.' But descending establishes that it is actual seeing, for through descending the matter is visible before the one descending. Once we interpret descending intellectually—'I shall descend to the end of their deeds'—the seeing is consequently intellectual too. Furthermore, 'He taught judges' is not an explanation of 'I shall see,' but of 'I shall descend': one must descend and see.

rows.en: 'Rather, this is a scribal adjustment, which they reversed to write in this way': In Beraishis Rabbah, Rabbi Simon said: This is a scribal adjustment, for the Shechinah was waiting for Avraham. It seems to me that this means: When Avraham our father saw the angels and thought they were guests, he asked the Name to wait for him until he brought the guests in, and He waited for him. When they turned from the place to which he had accompanied them and went to Sedom, He was still waiting for him. It should therefore have said, 'And ה׳ was still standing,' not 'Avraham was still standing.' Rather, this is a scribal adjustment, for it is not respectful toward Heaven to say, 'And ה׳ was still standing,' and so forth. The sequence of the verses is thus: 'Avraham went with them to send them off'; 'The men turned from there and went to Sedom, and Avraham was still standing before ה׳'; 'And ה׳ said: Shall I conceal from Avraham'; 'He said to him: The outcry of Sedom,' through 'And if not, I shall know'; 'Avraham approached and said,' and so forth. But Rashi's words imply that the scribal adjustment was only because the Shechinah came to Avraham, not he to the Shechinah; therefore it should have written 'And ה׳ was still standing,' and so forth. I do not understand this. What difference does it make whether Avraham went to the Shechinah or the Shechinah came to him? Suppose it had written, 'The Name came to Avraham, and Avraham arose and stood before ה׳,' and afterward, 'Avraham was still standing before ה׳'—would that not then have its ordinary meaning? Wherever 'scribal adjustment' occurs, its meaning is not, Heaven forbid, that they added to what is written in the Torah or changed what is written in it. Rather, they examined and found from the context of each of those verses that its principal intent was not as it appears from what is written in the scroll, but another aspect of meaning: it should have been written in one way rather than the other, but Scripture used a respectful substitute. They called them 'scribal adjustments' only because the scribes examined and explained that they are substitutions. These are Rashba's words. Rashi, however, added: 'This is a scribal adjustment which our Rabbis reversed to write in this way.' I discussed this at length on the verse 'Let me not see my misfortune'; see there.
rows.he: אלא תקון סופרים הוא זה שהפכוהו לכתוב כן. בב"ר א"ר סימון תקון סופרים הוא זה שהשכינה היתה ממתנת לאברהם ונר' לי שכך פירושו שבשעה שראה אברהם אבינו את המלאכים וחשב שהם אורחים בקש מהשם שימתין לו עד שיכניס את האורחים והיה ממתין לו וכשפנו ממקום שלוום והלכו לסדום עדיין הי' ממתין לו והיה ראוי לומר וה' עודנו עומד לא ואברהם עודנו עומד אלא תקון סופרים הוא זה שאין זה דרך כבוד כלפי מעלה לומר וה' עודנו עומד וגו' וסדר המקראות כן הוא ואברהם הולך עמם לשלחם ויפנו משם האנשים וילכו סדומה ואברהם עודנו עומד לפני ה' וה' אמר המכסה אני מאברהם ויאמר אליו זעקת סדום עד ואם לא אדעה ויגש אברהם ויאמר וגו' אבל מדברי רש"י משמע שהתקון של סופרים לא היה אלא מפני שהשכינה בא' אל אברהם ולא הוא אל השכינ' ולכן היה לו לכתוב וה' עודנו עומד וגו' ולא הבינותי זה דמה הפרש יש בין אם הלך אברהם אצל השכינ' או אם השכינה באה אליו הגע עצמך שהיה כותב ויבא השם אל אברהם ויקם אברהם ויעמד לפני ה' ואח"כ היה כותב ואברהם עודנו עומד לפני ה' לא היה אז כמשמעו ופי' תקון סופרי' בכל מקום אין הכונה בו חלילה שהוסיפו על מה שכתוב בתורה או ששינו ממה שכתוב בתורה אלא שהם דקדקו ומצאו לפי ענין כל אחד ואחד מן הכתובי' ההם שעקר הכונה לא היתה כמו שנר' ממ"ש בספר אלא צד כונה אחר' ולא היה לו לכתוב כן אלא כן אלא שכנה הכתוב ולא קראום תקון סופרים אלא שהם דקדקו ופירשו שהם כנוים לשון הרשב"א אבל רש"י הוסיף ואמר תיקון סופרים הוא זה שהפכוהו רבותינו לכתוב כן ובפסוק ואל ארא' ברעתי הארכתי בו וע"ש:

rows.en: Rashi: 'Still standing,' and so forth: 'But he did not go before Him; rather, the Shechinah came to him,' and so forth. These are Mizrachi's words: Rashi's words imply that the scribal adjustment was only because the Shechinah came to Avraham, not he to the Shechinah, and therefore it should have written 'And ה׳ was still standing,' and so forth. I do not understand: What difference does it make whether Avraham went to the Shechinah or the Shechinah came to him? Suppose it had written, 'The Name came to Avraham, and Avraham arose and stood before ה׳,' and afterward it wrote, 'Avraham was still standing before ה׳'—would that not then have its ordinary meaning? End of quotation. Gur Aryeh thought to answer, as follows: Its meaning is that, since the Shechinah came to Avraham, the expression 'still' does not fit Avraham. 'Still' implies that He is yet standing and has not departed from him; this can fit only the one who came to him and will eventually depart from him, so that 'still standing' applies, and so forth. End of quotation. But he has answered nothing, for his assertion is not necessary: it is not so that this expression can apply only to the one who came and will eventually depart. We can also say it about someone who was already sitting when another person came to him, and who arose before him and stood speaking with him, intending afterward to sit again. As long as he is standing and has not yet sat, one may say of the man who rose, 'So-and-so is still standing before so-and-so who came; the former has not yet sat.' This is exactly why Mizrachi carefully worded his example: Suppose it had written, 'The Name came to Avraham, and Avraham arose and stood before ה׳,' and afterward, 'Avraham was still standing before ה׳'—would that not then have its ordinary meaning? He means, rhetorically: If it then wrote 'Avraham was still standing,' meaning since he arose and had not yet sat, would that not have its ordinary meaning?

rows.en:
'But he did not go to stand before Him,' and so forth: This is in Beraishis Rabbah (49:7). Mizrachi asked: What difference is there between 'ה׳ was standing before Avraham' and 'Avraham was standing before ה׳'? Its meaning is, however, that after the Shechinah came to Avraham, 'still' cannot be said of Avraham. 'Still' implies that he is yet standing and has not departed from him. This expression can fit only the one who came to him and is eventually to depart from him; of him, 'still standing' applies. But how can one who did not come, and was already there, be described as 'still standing'? 'Still' applies only to one who will eventually depart, and this is said only of the one who came. Consider whether one could say, 'The tree is still standing before Reuven.' That would not fit, since it will not eventually depart. Here too it does not fit: Avraham did not come to stand before ה׳, so it is not speaking of someone who is to depart. Departure is spoken of only concerning one who first came: because he came from his place and remains waiting with the one to whom he came, 'still' applies to him, since he is lingering with him.

References: 49:7; Verse 20.

'A scribal adjustment': The meaning is not, Heaven forbid, that a scribe wrote it this way in the Torah—far be it to say so. Rather, the Torah wrote respectfully toward Heaven, as scribes customarily write respectfully. Just as the Torah speaks in human language, so it also wrote for you in the manner scribes customarily write and speak. Therefore they said, 'It is a scribal adjustment,' meaning that the Torah wrote this matter as a scribal adjustment, in the manner scribes customarily employ.

rows.en: 'Avraham entered into all these—to speak harshly, to conciliate, and to pray': This follows Rabbi Eliezer in Beraishis Rabbah: Whether I come for war, for conciliation, or for prayer, I come. Harsh words: 'Will You sweep away the righteous with the wicked?'—he stands in a contest in which justice is on his side. Conciliation: 'Will You destroy for the five?'—meaning, if nine remain in each city, You will join with them; this is beyond the strict letter of the law. Prayer: 'Perhaps forty will be found there,' so that four cities will be saved; or thirty and three will be saved; or twenty and two will be saved; or ten and one will be saved.

rows.en: 'He approached,' and so forth; 'for conciliation: Yehudah approached him': This is a scribal error; it should say, 'The children of Yehudah approached Yehoshua,' a verse in the book of Yehoshua. This is also the wording in Beraishis Rabbah, and it is the correct one. In 'Yehudah approached him,' although there is indeed conciliation, there is also prayer and warfare, for he spoke harshly to him. Why single it out for conciliation? Know that on that very verse, 'Yehudah approached him,' Beraishis Rabbah likewise interprets: We find an approaching for conciliation, for prayer, and for war; it brings these same examples and concludes, 'Yehudah entered into all of them'; see there. The reason Rashi brought the Midrash here but not there is that it is not necessary there: the plain meaning works well—'he approached him,' that is, came close to him, as someone speaking privately with another person draws near. Here, however, one cannot speak of Avraham approaching the Holy One, blessed is He, in that manner; therefore he needed the interpretation here.

'We find approaching,' and so forth: Here too there is warfare—'Will You sweep away the righteous with the wicked?'; conciliation—'I am dust and ashes'; and prayer—'Let not, please, anger be kindled,' and so forth, which is prayer, meaning, 'Let not Your anger be kindled.' But it appears to me that all three are within a single matter: he had three intentions in these words. Avraham's words were somewhat harsh, but also conciliatory, for he sought to conciliate Him when he said, 'Perhaps there are fifty righteous people,' asking the Holy One, blessed is He, to act for the righteous' sake. He also intended prayer, praying that the Holy One, blessed is He, do this by way of prayer. This is clear. Know that our Sages of blessed memory hinted in this Midrash at a very hidden matter: Avraham directed himself toward three Names, 'אל,' 'אלקים,' and 'ה׳.' Opposite the Name 'אלקים,' which is the attribute of judgment, he spoke harshly—warfare. Opposite the Name 'אל,' the attribute of kindness, he spoke conciliatory words. Prayer and mercy belong to ה׳, the unique Name. These correspond to 'the great, the mighty, and the awesome': warfare corresponds to 'the mighty'; he speaks conciliatory words corresponding to 'the great,' for on account of His greatness one should speak to Him conciliatorily, and on account of His greatness He does kindness; corresponding to 'the awesome,' one should pray in the manner of prayer. Understand this.

References: Verse 27; Verse 30; Verse 24; Beraishis Rabbah 49:8; Devarim 10:17.

rows.en: 'Ten righteous people for each city': He said 'within the city' with reference to Sedom, which was the principal city. We learn this from the Name's reply, 'If I find in Sedom.' rows.en: 'So You did to the generation of the Flood': The meaning is that people will say this, not that it is true. For afterward, on 'Perhaps ten will be found there,' Rashi also wrote that Avraham did not ask for fewer because in the generation of the Flood there were Noach, his sons and their wives, and they did not save their generation. Beraishis Rabbah likewise says this. But there is a difficulty: If so, the Name could say to him, 'Since this is not My practice, yet they say so anyway, then even if I do not put the righteous to death with the wicked, but the righteous are saved, they will still say that My practice is to sweep everyone away.' Furthermore, what does 'lest they say that this is His practice' mean, implying that otherwise He would also put the righteous to death? In the Flood He did not sweep away Noach and his sons; their righteousness stood for them and saved them, and had they not fallen short of ten, they would also have saved their generation. We must therefore say that 'Far be it from You to do such a thing' refers back: Far be it from You not to forgive the place in the merit of the righteous within it. For people will say that His practice is to sweep everyone away, righteous and wicked together. They do not know that those You swept away were wicked; rather, they think that righteous people too were swept away with them. Afterward, to make sense of 'to put the righteous to death with the wicked,' which has no connection with the preceding words—for until now he spoke only of the righteous saving the place, not of the righteous themselves being saved—Rashi added 'And if You say.' This continues until the other 'Far be it from You': If You say the righteous should not save the wicked, but You wish to bring a general destruction, putting the righteous to death with the wicked, far be it from You—shall the Judge of all the earth not exercise justice? After setting the verses' interpretation in order, Rashi returns to explain the word 'far be it.'

rows.en: 'Far be it from You—in the world to come': This is how I found it in most copies, but I have not heard its explanation. I did find in Beraishis Rabbah: Rabbi Abba said, 'Far be it, far be it,' twice—there is a desecration of the Name of Heaven in this matter. It seems to me that the two occurrences of 'far be it' indicate the extremity of the desecration. This can only be desecration of the Name of Heaven, which is exceptional among all transgressions in that it is not fully forgiven until after one's death—that is, in the world to come—as stated at the end of Yoma. If one transgressed a positive commandment and repented, he is forgiven immediately, as it is said, 'Return, wayward children; I shall heal your waywardness.' If one transgressed a prohibition and repented, repentance suspends and Yom Kippur atones, as it is said, 'For on this day He will atone for you.' If one transgressed offenses punishable by excision or death by the court and repented, repentance and Yom Kippur suspend, and sufferings cleanse, as it is said, 'I shall visit their transgression with the rod and their iniquity with plagues.' But for one who has desecrated the Name, neither repentance has the power to suspend, nor sufferings to cleanse, nor Yom Kippur to atone; rather, all together suspend, and death cleanses, as it is said, 'It was revealed in my ears by ה׳ of hosts: Surely this iniquity will not be atoned for until you die.' Thus 'in the world to come' means that he does not receive full forgiveness in this world through repentance, Yom Kippur, or sufferings, but in the world to come, that is, after death.

rows.en: Rashi: 'Far be it from You—in the world to come': Mizrachi and Gur Aryeh offered explanations, but it appears to me that this is the meaning. Avraham understood that the judgment the blessed Name wished to carry out against Sedom was a decree that they be cut off from this world and from the world to come, having no share in the world to come. If He put the righteous to death with them, then one judgment would apply to them all: the righteous would be like the wicked, cut off even from the world to come. Therefore Avraham, peace be upon him, said 'far be it' twice: It would be profane for You in this world, when people see the righteous perish from this world with the wicked and say that this is His practice; and it would also be profane for You in the world to come, when the other righteous people there see that these righteous people do not come to them in the Garden of Eden—for they too know there what occurs in this world—and they too say: Certainly they perished and were cut off with the wicked of their generation. It would be, as it were, profane for You in the world to come, for they too would say, Heaven forbid, that this is His practice. This would be desecration of the Name even in the world to come. This appears to me to be its plain meaning, with no need for their strained explanations.

rows.en:
'This is His practice': Although this did not happen, since Noach was saved, so that there is no desecration of the Name—Mizrachi's objection—people will say: It is impossible that there were no other righteous people in the generation of the Flood. Rather, Noach and his sons remained because of their exceptional righteousness, or to preserve the species so that the world would not be entirely destroyed. If He destroys everyone here, people will say that His practice is to destroy all. Do not ask: If destroying the righteous and wicked is improper, He should not do it for that reason; why is the reason 'lest they say this is His practice' needed? Avraham certainly knew that there were no righteous people there, but there were people who appeared righteous and were not. Therefore every occurrence of 'righteous people' concerning Sedom is written defectively, meaning people not fully righteous, but appearing righteous. Because it would be seen as having happened three times—the Flood, the Dispersion, and here—people would not attribute it to their only seeming righteous rather than truly being so, but would say this is His practice. After a third occurrence, they would say that a pattern is established, and such is His practice. Nor is there a difficulty from Mizrachi's further objection: Even without this, people would say of the Flood and the Dispersion that He swept everyone away, righteous and wicked, although it was not so; if so, now too they would say so even if He did not sweep away righteous and wicked. For now, once it has happened three times, they would no longer attribute it to any particular cause and say this is not His practice, but that in the Flood it was because of sexual transgression, a sin through which He kills good and evil alike; or that in the Dispersion there was a reason, for all sinned, or some other reason. Rather, once they see a pattern established, they will attribute it to no particular cause, but simply say this is His practice.

'Far be it from You—in the world to come': In Tanchuma the reading is, 'Far be it from You in the world to come.' It appears that this means: Even in the world to come it would be profane for You. If You do not exercise justice in this world, it is profane for You forever. Not only in this world, where it is certainly profane for You because the deed takes place here, but even in the world to come it would be profane for You if there is no justice in this world. That is, the deed You do in this world, in not exercising justice, would be profane for You in the world to come. The reason is that judgment is deep—who can find it? Concerning this they said in Pesachim that the depth of judgment is concealed from human beings. Its depth indicates its elevated quality, reaching the world to come. Therefore, if He does not exercise justice, it would be profane even in the world to come. This is very sound. Some explain 'the world to come' as the coming generations: this is called the world that is to come.

References: Old Tanchuma, Vayeira, 11; Based on Koheles 7:24; Beginning of 54b; Chizkuni.

AND THE ETERNAL SAID. I.e., to the host of heaven standing by Him, or to the angel messengers.
It is possible that the word amar (He said) refers to thought, meaning that He thought He should not keep it hidden from Abraham on account of these reasons. Similarly: I ‘said,’ in the noontide of my days I shall go; And he ‘said’ to slay David. Likewise all expressions of speaking within the heart refer to thought.

rows.en:
'Avraham will indeed become': A Midrash of Aggadah explains, 'The memory of the righteous is for a blessing': since He mentioned him, He blessed him. The plain meaning of Scripture is: Shall I conceal it from him, when he is beloved before Me, destined to become a mighty nation? These are Rashi's words. The correct interpretation is that the blessed Name spoke in honor of Avraham. He said: He is destined to become a great and mighty nation, and his memory among his descendants and among all the nations of the earth will be for a blessing. Therefore I shall not conceal it from him, for the coming generations would say, 'How did He conceal it from him?' or, 'How was the righteous man cruel toward his neighbors dwelling beside him, showing no mercy and not praying for them at all?' Disclosing it to him is good and fitting, for I know that he recognizes and knows that I am ה׳, who loves righteousness and justice—that is, that I exercise judgment only with righteousness. Therefore he will command his children and household after him to hold fast to My way. Thus, if they may be acquitted through righteousness and justice, he will pray before Me to leave them, and that is good; and if they are completely guilty, he too will desire their judgment. It is therefore fitting that he enter the counsel of ה׳.

Source reference: Rashi on Genesis 18:18.

FOR I HAVE KNOWN HIM (‘YEDATIV’), TO THE END (‘LEMA’AN’) THAT HE MAY COMMAND HIS CHILDREN. Rashi comments: “For I have known him, as the Targum takes it, is an expression denoting affection, just as A kinsman (‘moda’) of her husband’s; And I know thee. Still the main connotation of all these expressions is that of knowing, for he who holds a person in affection and draws him to himself knows him well and is familiar with him. But if you explain it as the Targum does — i.e., “I know that he will command his children” — then the word lema’an (to the end) does not fit into the sense.”
It is possible that the word yedativ means “I have raised him and elevated him so that he shall command his children after him to do that which is right before Me, and therefore I will make him a great and mighty nation so that they should serve Me.” In a similar sense are the verses: I know thee (‘yedaticha’) by name; What is man, that Thou knowest him? Or the verse may be stating, I know that he will command, and in a similar sense is the verse, So that thine ox and thine ass may have rest (lema’an yanuach), meaning that he may have rest.
The correct interpretation appears to me to be that the word yedativ literally means “knowing.” He is thus alluding that G-d’s knowledge, which is synonymous with His Providence in the lower world, is to guard the species, and even the children of men are subject despite it to the chance occurrences until the time of their visitation comes. But as regards His pious, He directs His Providence to know each one individually so that His watch constantly attaches to him, His knowledge and remembrance of him never departs, as it says: He withdraweth not His eyes from the righteous. There are many verses on this theme, as it is written, Behold, the eye of the Eternal is toward them that fear Him, and other verses besides.
rows.he: כִּי יְדַעְתִּיו לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר יְצַוֶּה לְשׁוֹן רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית י"ח:י"ט), "אֲרִי יְדַעְתִּנֵּיהּ" כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ, לְשׁוֹן חִבָּה, כְּמוֹ "מוֹדָע לְאִישָׁהּ" (רות ב א), "וָאֵדָעֲךָ" (שמות לג יז). אָמְנָם עִקַּר כֻּלָּם לְשׁוֹן יְדִיעָה, שֶׁהַמְחַבֵּב אֶת הָאָדָם וּמְקָרְבוֹ אֶצְלוֹ יוֹדְעוֹ וּמַכִּירוֹ. וְאִם תְּפָרְשֵׁהוּ יוֹדֵעַ אֲנִי בּוֹ שֶׁיְּצַוֶּה אֶת בָּנָיו, אֵין "לְמַעַן" נוֹפֵל עַל הַלָּשׁוֹן. וְיִתָּכֵן שֶׁיִּהְיֶה "יְדַעְתִּיו", גִּדַּלְתִּיו וְרוֹמַמְתִּיו בַּעֲבוּר אֲשֶׁר יְצַוֶּה אֶת בָּנָיו אַחֲרָיו לַעֲשׂוֹת אֶת הַיָּשָׁר לְפָנַי, וּלְכָךְ אֲשִׂימֶנּוּ לְגוֹי גָּדוֹל וְעָצוּם שֶׁיַּעַבְדוּנִי, וְכָמוֹהוּ "יְדַעְתִּיךָ בְשֵׁם" (שמות לג יב), "מָה אָדָם וַתֵּדָעֵהוּ" (תהלים קמד ג). אוֹ יֹאמַר יְדַעְתִּיו שֶׁיְּצַוֶּה, וְכֵן "לְמַעַן יָנוּחַ שׁוֹרְךָ וַחֲמֹרֶךָ" (שמות כג יב), שֶׁיָּנוּחַ. וְהַנָּכוֹן בְּעֵינַי שֶׁהִיא יְדִיעָה בּוֹ מַמָּשׁ, יִרְמֹז כִּי יְדִיעַת הַשֵּׁם שֶׁהִיא הַשְׁגָּחָתוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַשָּׁפָל הִיא לִשְׁמֹר הַכְּלָלִים, וְגַם בְּנֵי הָאָדָם מֻנָּחִים בּוֹ לַמִּקְרִים עַד בֹּא עֵת פְּקֻדָּתָם, אֲבָל בַּחֲסִידָיו יָשׂוּם אֵלָיו לִבּוֹ לָדַעַת אוֹתוֹ בִּפְרָט, לִהְיוֹת שְׁמִירָתוֹ דְּבֵקָה בּוֹ תָּמִיד, לֹא תִּפָּרֵד הַיְּדִיעָה וְהַזְּכִירָה מִמֶּנּוּ כְּלָל, כְּטַעַם "לֹא יִגְרַע מִצַּדִּיק עֵינָיו" (איוב לו ז). וּבָאוּ מִזֶּה פְּסוּקִים רַבִּים, כְּדִכְתִיב (תהלים לג יח) "הִנֵּה עֵין ה' אֶל יְרֵאָיו" וְזוּלַת זֶה:

translatorNotes.en: Ruth 2:1.
Exodus 33:17.
Our Rashi has a different text. See notes in my Hebrew commentary, p. 110. See also Note 125 further.
Exodus 33:12. The sense would thus be: “I have made thee great in name.”
Psalms 144:3. The sense here then would be: “What is man before Thee that Thou hast given him greatness?”

Ramban thus differs with Rashi, who said that if you take the sense of the verse to be, “I know of him that he will command,” then the word lema’an does not fit the context. Ramban proceeds to show from Exodus 23:12 that the words lema’an yanuach mean she’yanuach (that he may rest); here likewise, lema’an asher yetzaveh means she’yetzaveh (that he will command). Thus, the word lema’an is seen to fit into the context.
Exodus 23:12. See Note above.
Psalms 33:18. See Moreh Nebuchim III, 51, where Rambam’s theory on Divine Providence is seen to be similar to that which Ramban expresses here.

rows.en:
'And ה׳ said: The outcry of Sedom and Amorah': Rashi says: 'And ה׳ said' to Avraham, carrying out what He had said, that He would not conceal it from him. Rabbi Avraham said that the verse 'The men turned away from there' was inserted between the statements to inform us that, when they came to Sedom, the Name then told Avraham, 'The outcry of Sedom and Amorah has become great.' All the commentators likewise understand Him to be speaking with Avraham. According to this, the correct understanding of 'The men turned away from there' is that when the Name told Avraham, as the men journeyed from him, 'The outcry of Sedom and Amorah has become great,' Avraham stood before Him in prayer and supplication to forgive them and to give him permission to speak. He prolonged his prayer until the men came to Sedom; then Avraham approached and said, 'Will You indeed sweep away?' Or its meaning may be that Scripture returns to explain 'he was still standing before ה׳': Avraham approached and said, 'Will You indeed sweep away?' He prolonged his supplication before Him each time, saying, 'Let the anger of ה׳ not be kindled,' and each time he again directed his mind toward prophecy until he heard an answer to his words from the mouth of the Holy One, blessed is He. They continued with this throughout the day; ה׳ went away in the evening when He finished speaking to Avraham, and the two angels came to Sedom. 'The outcry of Sedom and Amorah' is the outcry of the oppressed, who cry out and plead for help against the force of their wickedness. Scripture might fittingly have said, 'I have heard the outcry of Sedom and Amorah, for it has become great,' or, 'The outcry of Sedom and Amorah is great, and their sin is very grave.' But the meaning of Scripture is: With the outcry of Sedom and Amorah and their sin having grown very great, I shall descend and see whether all have sinned in these matters; if not, I shall know who the sinners are. As for descending and seeing, Rashi said in the manner of interpretation: He taught that capital cases must not be decided except through seeing. In the plain meaning, because the Holy One, blessed is He, wished to reveal the matter of Sedom to Avraham and inform him that none among them did good, He told him, 'The outcry of Sedom and Amorah has become great; I shall descend to see'—that is, I have come to judge. If they have sinned, I shall make an end of them; and if not, I shall know what to do with them, 'visiting their transgression with the rod and their iniquity with plagues.' He informed him that their judgment had not yet been completed, and that He would now take account of their sin and judge them. This is like 'ה׳ looked down from heaven upon human beings, to see whether there was anyone understanding, seeking God; all have turned aside, together they have become corrupt' (Tehillim 14:2–3). Rabbi Avraham spoke here of a secret, 'taking satisfaction in the offspring of foreigners.' I shall hint to you at the view of those who have received the truth. Our Rabbis interpreted the verse 'For behold, ה׳ goes out from His place, and descends and treads upon the heights of the earth' (Michah 1:3): He goes out and moves from one attribute to another, going out from the attribute of mercy and coming to the attribute of judgment. This matter is likewise: 'And ה׳ said' in His heart, 'The outcry of Sedom and Amorah has become great; I shall descend' from the attribute of mercy to the attribute of judgment, 'and see' with mercy whether 'according to its outcry that has come to Me' through the attribute of judgment 'they have done'—then complete destruction; 'and if not, I shall know' and have mercy, as in 'And God knew' (Shemos 2:25). After Scripture related the knowledge of the Most High, it returned to the original matter and related the event: the men who had looked toward Sedom to go there, and whom Avraham had accompanied, arrived there. From when they parted from him until they arrived there, Avraham was still standing before Him, for He had called him and told him that these messengers were the angels sent to destroy the place, as He had said. Scripture did not need to explain when he stood before Him, for from the time He said, 'Shall I conceal from Avraham?' it is known that He told him.

Additional references in the supplied Hebrew: Rashi on Genesis 18:20; Ibn Ezra on Genesis 18:10 (the citation as supplied); Jerusalem Talmud, Taanis, chapter 2; Zohar 105 and 106.

וְכֵן דַּעַת כָּל הַמְּפָרְשִׁים כִּי עִם אַבְרָהָם יְדַבֵּר, וּלְפִי זֶה הַנָּכוֹן בַּפָּסוּק "וַיִּפְנוּ מִשָּׁם הָאֲנָשִׁים" לוֹמַר כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר אָמַר הַשֵּׁם לְאַבְרָהָם בִּנְסֹעַ הָאֲנָשִׁים מִמֶּנּוּ "זַעֲקַת סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה כִּי רָבָּה", עָמַד אַבְרָהָם בִּתְפִלָּה וּתְחִנָּה לְפָנָיו לִמְחֹל לָהֶם וְלָתֵת לוֹ רְשׁוּת לְדַבֵּר, וְהֶאֱרִיךְ בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ עַד שֶׁבָּאוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים סְדֹמָה, וְאָז נִגַּשׁ אַבְרָהָם וְאָמַר, "הַאַף תִּסְפֶּה". אוֹ יִהְיֶה פֵּרוּשׁוֹ שֶׁשָּׁב לְבָאֵר "עוֹדֶנּוּ עֹמֵד לִפְנֵי ה'", כִּי נִגַּשׁ אַבְרָהָם וְאָמַר "הַאַף תִּסְפֶּה". וְהִנֵּה הֶאֱרִיךְ בִּתְחִנָּה לְפָנָיו בְּכָל פַּעַם לֵאמֹר "אַל יִחַר אַף ה'", וְהָיָה עוֹד מְכַוֵּן דַּעְתּוֹ בְּכָל פַּעַם לִנְבוּאָה עַד שֶׁשָּׁמַע תְּשׁוּבָה לִדְבָרָיו מִפִּיו שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, וְהֶאֱרִיכוּ כָּל הַיּוֹם בָּזֶה, וַיֵּלֶךְ ה' בָּעֶרֶב כַּאֲשֶׁר כִּלָּה לְדַבֵּר אֶל אַבְרָהָם, וּבָאוּ שְׁנֵי הַמַּלְאָכִים סְדֹמָה: זַעֲקַת סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה הִיא זַעֲקַת עֲשׁוּקִים יִזְעֲקוּ וִישַׁוְּעוּ מִזְּרוֹעַ רִשְׁעָתָם. וְהָיָה רָאוּי שֶׁיֹּאמַר הַכָּתוּב זַעֲקַת סְדוֹם וַעֲמֹרָה שָׁמַעְתִּי כִּי רָבָּה, אוֹ שֶׁיֹּאמַר זַעֲקַת סְדוֹם וַעֲמֹרָה רָבָּה וְחַטָּאתָם כָּבְדָה מְאֹד, אֲבָל עִנְיַן הַכָּתוּב, זַעֲקַת סְדוֹם וַעֲמֹרָה וְחַטָּאתָם שֶׁגָּדְלוּ מְאֹד אֵרֵד וְאֶרְאֶה אִם כֻּלָּם חָטְאוּ בָּהֶם, וְאִם לֹא אֵדָעָה מִי הַחוֹטְאִים. וְעִנְיַן הַיְּרִידָה וְהָרְאִיָּה אָמַר רַשִׁ"י בְּדֶרֶךְ הַדְּרָשׁ, לִמֵּד שֶׁלֹּא יִפְסְקוּ דִּינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת אֶלָּא בִּרְאִיָּה. וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ הַפְּשָׁט, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁרָצָה הקב"ה לְגַלּוֹת לְאַבְרָהָם עִנְיַן סְדוֹם וּלְהוֹדִיעוֹ כִּי אֵין בָּהֶם עֹשֶׂה טוֹב, אָמַר אֵלָיו זַעֲקַת סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה כִּי רָבָּה, אֵרֵד לִרְאוֹת, כְּלוֹמַר בָּאתִי לִשְׁפֹּט, אִם חָטְאוּ אֶעֱשֶׂה בָּהֶם כָּלָה, וְאִם לֹא אֵדָעָה מָה אֶעֱשֶׂה בָּהֶם, וּפָקַדְתִּי בְשֵׁבֶט פִּשְׁעָם וּבִנְגָעִים עֲוֹנָם, הוֹדִיעוֹ כִּי אֵין עוֹד נִגְמַר דִּינָם, וְכִי עַתָּה יִפְקֹד עֲוֹנָם וְיִשְׁפֹּט אוֹתָם. וְזֶה כִּלְשׁוֹן "ה' מִשָּׁמַיִם הִשְׁקִיף עַל בְּנֵי אָדָם לִרְאוֹת הֲיֵשׁ מַשְׂכִּיל דֹּרֵשׁ אֶת אֱלֹהִים הַכֹּל סָר יַחְדָּיו נֶאֱלָחוּ" (תהלים יד ב ג). וְרַבִּי אַבְרָהָם אָמַר בּוֹ סוֹד מִיַּלְדֵי נָכְרִים יַסְפִּיקוּ בּוֹ. וַאֲנִי אֶרְמֹז לְךָ דַּעַת מְקַבְּלֵי הָאֱמֶת, דָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ (ירושלמי תענית פ"ב) בַּפָּסוּק "כִּי הִנֵּה ה' יֹצֵא מִמְּקוֹמוֹ וְיָרַד וְדָרַךְ עַל בָּמֳתֵי אָרֶץ" (מיכה א ג), יוֹצֵא וּבָא לוֹ מִמִּדָּה לְמִדָּה, יוֹצֵא מִמִּדַּת רַחֲמִים וּבָא לוֹ לְמִדַּת הַדִּין. וְכֵן הָעִנְיָן הַזֶּה, וַיֹּאמֶר ה' אֶל לִבּוֹ זַעֲקַת סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה כִּי רָבָּה, אֵרֵד מִמִּדַּת רַחֲמִים אֶל מִדַּת הַדִּין (זהר קה), וְאֶרְאֶה בְּרַחֲמִים אִם כְּצַעֲקָתָהּ הַבָּאָה אֵלַי בְּמִדַּת הַדִּין עָשׂוּ כָּלָה (שם קו), וְאִם לֹא אֵדָעָה וַאֲרַחֵם, כְּדֶרֶךְ "וַיֵּדַע אֱלֹהִים" (שמות ב כה). וְאַחַר שֶׁסִּפֵּר הַכָּתוּב דַּעַת הָעֶלְיוֹן, חָזַר אֶל הָעִנְיָן הָרִאשׁוֹן וְסִפֵּר בְּמַעֲשֶׂה כִּי הָאֲנָשִׁים אֲשֶׁר הִשְׁקִיפוּ עַל פְּנֵי סְדוֹם לָלֶכֶת שָׁמָּה וְשִׁלְּחָם אַבְרָהָם, הִגִּיעוּ שָׁמָּה, וְאַבְרָהָם מֵעֵת הִפָּרְדָם מִמֶּנּוּ וְעַד הַגִּיעָם שָׁם עוֹדֶנּוּ עוֹמֵד לְפָנָיו, כִּי קְרָאוֹ וְהִגִּיד לוֹ כִּי הַמַּלְאָכִים הֵם הַשְּׁלוּחִים הָאֵלֶּה לְהַשְׁחִית הַמָּקוֹם כַּאֲשֶׁר אָמַר. וְלֹא הֻצְרַךְ לְפָרֵשׁ מָתַי עָמַד לְפָנָיו, כִּי מֵעֵת שֶׁאָמַר "הַמְכַסֶּה אֲנִי מֵאַבְרָהָם" נוֹדַע שֶׁהִגִּיד לוֹ:

notes.en: Ramban offers two sequences for Avraham's prayer and mentions 'ה׳ went away in the evening.' The reference to Ibn Ezra 18:10 is the reference supplied in the Hebrew; it is not silently corrected here. 'Taking satisfaction in the offspring of foreigners' is polemical language alluding to Yeshaya 2:6, not praise of foreign teaching. Ibn Ezra's words are discussed within Ramban's commentary, not as an independent commentary added to the reading.
notes.he: הרמב״ן מציע שתי דרכים לסדר תפילת אברהם, ומזכיר את ׳וילך ה׳ בערב׳. ההפניה לאבן עזרא י״ח:י׳ היא ההפניה שנמסרה בנוסח העברי; אין מתקנים אותה כאן בשתיקה. ׳מילדי נכרים יספיקו בו׳ היא לשון פולמוס המרמזת לישעיה ב׳ ו׳, ולא שבח לתורה זרה. דברי אבן עזרא נידונים בתוך פירוש הרמב״ן, ולא כפירוש עצמאי שנוסף לקריאה.

rows.en:
AND ABRAHAM DREW NEAR AND SAID, WILT THOU ALSO SWEEP AWAY THE RIGHTEOUS WITH THE WICKED? The anger of the Holy One, blessed be He, is His attribute of justice. Now Abraham thought that this would sweep away the righteous with the wicked, not knowing of G-d’s thoughts in which He thought of them with His mercies, as I have explained. Therefore, Abraham said that it is proper and good that He should forgive the entire place because of the fifty righteous inhabitants, but it is inconceivable even according to the Divine attribute of Justice to slay the righteous with the wicked, for if so the righteous will be as the wicked, and they will say, It is vain to serve G-d. And all the more is this inconceivable according to the Divine attribute of Mercy since He is the Judge of all the earth, and He does justice, even as it is said, And the Eternal of hosts is exalted through justice, and we say in our prayers, “The King of judgment.” This is the significance of the double use of the expression, It is unworthy of Thee. And the Holy One, blessed be He, conceded that He would forgive the entire place for the sake of the fifty righteous, for He will conduct Himself towards them with the attribute of Mercy.
What informs you of all this is the fact vayomer hashem (And the Eternal said) is written with the Tetragrammaton, and all references by Abraham to the Divine Name are written Ado-noy. This has now been clarified.

rows.en:
FIFTY RIGHTEOUS. Rashi wrote: “Ten righteous men for each city. Wilt thou destroy on account of the five. Nine for each city, and You, the All-Righteous One of the Universe, will be counted with them [to make up the original number of ten]. Perhaps there shall be found there forty. Then let four cities be saved. So, too, thirty will save three of them, twenty will save two of them, and ten will save one of them. And he did not plead for less than ten since in the generation of the flood there were eight righteous people, and they could not save their generation. For nine, in association with G-d, he had already pleaded but found no acceptance.” All these are the words of the Rabbi, of blessed memory.
But I wonder: If so, what is this prayer and supplication which he pleads each and every time, saying, oh let not the Lord be angry; Behold, now, I have taken upon me to speak? It is proper that forty should save four cities, and thirty and twenty should save in proportion, just as fifty would save five! Similarly, concerning that which Rashi said, “for nine in association with G-d he had already pleaded but found no acceptance,” it may be asked: When he pleaded about forty-five, [i.e., to save all five cities by having nine righteous men for each city] in association [with G-d to make up ten], and he did not find forty-five, but perhaps he might have found there nine! Now it would seem that the intention of the Rabbi is that many righteous people can effect a proportionately greater salvation than a few righteous people can, just as the Sages have said: “A few who fulfill the commandments of the Torah cannot compare with the many who fulfill the commandments of the Torah.” And thus, the Holy One, blessed be He, having conceded that forty-five righteous men in association with the All-Righteous One of the Universe would save all the five cities just as if there were the entire fifty, it follows that when forty righteous men save four cities, those cities will also be saved through association with the Righteous One, exalted be He; and the same applies to thirty, twenty, and ten, since He has already conceded this association. [Thus, thirty-six would save four, twenty-seven three, eighteen two, and nine one]. And in case you say that He conceded only the case of forty-five because they are many, and perhaps He might not concede the principle of association with the few, as we have said, the refutation is that it is proper for the righteousness of G-d to associate even with the few and save [as many of the cities as possible] since He had conceded the principle of association, for He would not distinguish between the many and the few. This is the opinion of the Rabbi.
But the way of the simple meaning of the verses is smooth. First Abraham said fifty in order to give a perfect number of ten for each city, and then he decreased the number as much as possible, and each time he thought to save all five cities. And I do not know who brought the Rabbi to that which he said.
rows.he: חֲמִשִּׁים צַדִּיקִים כָּתַב רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית י"ח:כ"ד), עֲשָׂרָה לְכָל כְּרַךְ וּכְרַךְ, "הֲתַשְׁחִית בַּחֲמִשָּׁה", תִּשְׁעָה לְכָל כְּרַךְ וּכְרַךְ, וְאַתָּה צַדִּיקוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם תִּצְטָרֵף עִמָּהֶם, "אוּלַי יִמָּצְאוּן שָׁם אַרְבָּעִים", וְיִמָּלְטוּ אַרְבָּעָה כְּרַכִּים, וְכֵן שְׁלֹשִׁים יַצִּילוּ שְׁלֹשָׁה וְעֶשְׂרִים יַצִּילוּ שְׁנַיִם וַעֲשָׂרָה יַצִּילוּ אֶחָד. וְלֹא בִּקֵּשׁ עַל פָּחוֹת מֵעֲשָׂרָה, שֶׁדּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל הָיוּ שְׁמֹנָה צַדִּיקִים וְלֹא הִצִּילוּ עַל דּוֹרָן, וְתִשְׁעָה עַל יְדֵי צֵרוּף כְּבָר בִּקֵּשׁ וְלֹא מָצָא. כָּל אֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי הָרַב זַ"ל. וַאֲנִי תָּמֵהַּ, אִם כֵּן מָה הַתְּפִלָּה וְהַתְּחִנָּה הַזֹּאת אֲשֶׁר הָיָה מִתְחַנֵּן בְּכָל פַּעַם וּפַעַם, "אַל נָא יִחַר לַאדֹנָי", וְ"הִנֵּה נָא הוֹאַלְתִּי", וַהֲלֹא רָאוּי הוּא שֶׁיִּהְיוּ אַרְבָּעִים מַצִּילִין אַרְבָּעָה, וּשְׁלֹשִׁים וְהָעֶשְׂרִים יַצִּילוּ לְפִי חֶשְׁבּוֹן כַּאֲשֶׁר הַחֲמִשִּׁים יַצִּילוּ חָמֵשׁ. וְכֵן מָה שֶׁאָמַר כִּי תִּשְׁעָה עַל יְדֵי צֵרוּף כְּבָר בִּקֵּשׁ וְלֹא מָצָא, וַהֲלֹא לְאַרְבָּעִים וַחֲמִשָּׁה הָיָה מְבַקֵּשׁ הַצֵּרוּף וְלֹא הָיוּ שָׁם אַרְבָּעִים וַחֲמִשָּׁה, אֲבָל תִּשְׁעָה אוּלַי יִמָּצְאוּן שָׁם. וְהִנֵּה דַּעַת הָרַב לוֹמַר שֶׁהָרַבִּים רְאוּיִין לְהַצָּלָה גְּדוֹלָה יוֹתֵר מֵאֲשֶׁר יַצִּילוּ הַמּוּעָטִים אֲפִלּוּ הַצָּלָה מוּעֶטֶת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (ת"כ בחקותי) אֵינוֹ דּוֹמֶה מוּעָטִין הָעוֹשִׂין אֶת הַתּוֹרָה לִמְרֻבִּים הָעוֹשִׂין אֶת הַתּוֹרָה. וְהִנֵּה הוֹדָה הקב"ה שֶׁיַּצִּילוּ אַרְבָּעִים וַחֲמִשָּׁה בְּצֵרוּף צַדִּיקוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם כָּל הַכְּרַכִּין כְּאִלּוּ הָיוּ חֲמִשִּׁים שְׁלֵמִין, וּמֵעַתָּה כְּשֶׁיִּהְיוּ מ' צַדִּיקִים מַצִּילִין אַרְבָּעָה אַף בְּצֵרוּף הַצַּדִּיק יִתְעַלֶּה יִנָּצְלוּ, וְכֵן הַשְּׁלֹשִׁים וְהָעֶשְׂרִים וְהָעֲשָׂרָה, שֶׁכְּבָר הוֹדָה בַּצֵּרוּף הַזֶּה. וְאִם תֹּאמַר שֶׁהוֹדָה בּוֹ עִם אַרְבָּעִים וַחֲמִשָּׁה שֶׁהֵם רַבִּים, וְשֶׁמָּא לֹא יוֹדֶה בַּצֵּרוּף עִם הַמּוּעָטִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ, צִדְקַת ה' רְאוּיָה הִיא לְהִצְטָרֵף וּלְהַצִּיל, כֵּיוָן שֶׁהוֹדָה שֶׁלֹּא יַבְדִּיל בֵּין רַב לִמְעָט. זֶה דַּעַת הָרַב. וְדֶרֶךְ פְּשַׁט הַכְּתוּבִים סְלוּלָה, שֶׁאָמַר תְּחִלָּה חֲמִשִּׁים לָתֵת חֶשְׁבּוֹן שָׁלֵם שֶׁל עֲשָׂרָה לְכָל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד, וְחָזַר וּפָחַת כְּמוֹ שֶׁיָּכוֹל, וּלְהַצִּיל הַכֹּל הָיָה אוֹמֵר. וְלֹא יָדַעְתִּי מִי הִכְנִיסוֹ לָרַב בַּמֶּה שֶׁאָמַר:

Why then did Abraham not plead for nine men who, in association with G-d, would be ten, and thus save one city, for the principle of using G-d as a tenth was not declared invalid; rather, it was previously inapplicable since there were not forty-five righteous inhabitants.
Rashi.
Sifra, Leviticus 26:8. The wording of the quotations used here is that of Rashi in his commentary to the Torah. (Ibid.)
“And thus.” The Tur quoting Ramban writes, “Perhaps.”

In other words, having admitted the principle of association in the case of forty-five, there could not be any difference between a larger and smaller group of righteous men with respect to the principle of association. Hence Abraham did not have to ask for nine, for in association with G-d there would be ten, and one city would be saved. But without the principle of association there might be a difference between a larger and smaller group. Hence Abraham had to ask for forty, thirty, twenty and ten. All this is to satisfactorily explain the interpretation of Rashi. Ramban’s own position is made clear further in the text.
Rashi.
See Proverbs 15:19.

rows.en:
WITHIN THE CITY. Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra explained that [these men for whose sake the cities were to be saved] fear G-d publicly. In a similar sense is the verse: Run ye to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem.
The correct interpretation appears to me to be that Abraham said, within the city, meaning that even if they are strangers therein, it is fitting that they save it. He said this on account of Lot, and he thought that perhaps there are others there.
rows.he: בְּתוֹךְ הָעִיר פֵּרֵשׁ רַבִּי אַבְרָהָם שֶׁיִּהְיוּ יְרֵאִים אֶת הַשֵּׁם בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא, וְכֵן "שׁוֹטְטוּ בְּחֻצוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַם" (ירמיהו ה א). וְהַנָּכוֹן בְּעֵינַי כִּי אַבְרָהָם אָמַר "בְּתוֹךְ הָעִיר", לֵאמֹר שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ יִהְיוּ נָכְרִים בְּתוֹכָהּ רָאוּי שֶׁיַּצִּילוּהָ. וְאָמַר זֶה בַּעֲבוּר לוֹט, וְחָשַׁב אוּלַי יֵשׁ אֲחֵרִים שָׁם:
